title: Low-VOC Carpet: Does New Carpet Smell Go Away and Is It Safe?
meta: New carpet smell fades in 2 to 3 days and comes from the backing, not the fiber. Wills Flooring on low-VOC labels, safety and airing out a Sammamish home.
keywords: low VOC carpet, does new carpet smell go away, is new carpet smell toxic, Green Label Plus carpet, new carpet off-gassing how long, carpet installation Sammamish WA

blocks.lead: Yes, new carpet smell goes away, usually within two to three days with the windows open, and carpet that carries the CRI Green Label Plus mark has been tested to emit very low levels of VOCs.
blocks.detail: The smell is mostly a compound called 4-PC from the latex that holds the backing together, at concentrations far below any health threshold. It is unpleasant, not dangerous. The pad and any adhesive can add more, and those are the parts you can control.

blocks.html: This question comes up most in Sammamish for a reason. Klahanie, Trossachs and the newer plateau neighborhoods are full of tightly built 1990s to 2010s homes with heat-recovery ventilators and windows that stay shut from October to April. A family with a baby, a dog and someone with asthma orders carpet for four bedrooms, and the smell has nowhere to go. Here is what the smell is, what the labels mean, what the research says about safety, and how to clear it out of a sealed-up house in a rainy week.

blocks.text: Where the new carpet smell comes from

items.title: Latex backing (4-PC)
items.text: Almost all broadloom carpet has a secondary backing glued on with styrene-butadiene latex. A by-product of that latex, 4-phenylcyclohexene, is what you smell. Human noses detect it at astonishingly low levels, which is why a room can smell strongly while instruments barely register it.

items.title: The pad
items.text: Rebond pad is made from recycled foam scraps bonded with adhesive and can carry its own odor. Felt, fiber and some virgin foam pads emit less. Pad is usually the second biggest contributor and the easiest thing to upgrade.

items.title: Adhesive (glue-down only)
items.text: Glue-down installations add carpet adhesive to the mix. Nearly every residential job in Sammamish is stretch-in over pad with tack strip, which uses no adhesive at all, so this one rarely applies to a house.

items.title: The fiber itself
items.text: Nylon, polyester, triexta and wool fibers contribute very little to the smell. Topical stain treatments applied at the mill can add a faint chemical note for a day. The fiber is not the problem people assume it is.

blocks.text: Is it actually safe? What the research says

blocks.html: The honest summary: measured VOC emissions from new carpet are low, they peak in the first 24 to 72 hours, and they drop to background levels within a couple of weeks. The compound behind the smell, 4-PC, has been studied since the 1980s and has not been shown to cause harm at the levels found in homes. That said, three groups deserve extra care. People with asthma or chemical sensitivity can react to the smell itself even when the concentration is medically trivial. Newborns spend hours a day inches from the floor. And an unrelated worry got attached to carpet in the last decade: PFAS-based stain treatments. Most major mills stopped using PFAS on residential carpet several years ago, and we can confirm it product by product. For a deeper look at fiber choices, see our comparison of nylon, polyester, triexta and wool.

blocks.text: How to clear the smell from a sealed-up plateau house

items.text: Schedule the job for a stretch when you can run the house a few degrees warmer and open windows for an hour or two, even in the rain. Warm air speeds off-gassing; ventilation removes it.

Open windows on two sides of the house for cross-flow. If you have an HRV or ERV, set it to its highest continuous setting. Run bathroom fans. Vacuum the new carpet once the crew leaves to pull loose fiber.
Keep the HRV on high and the thermostat at 72 or above. Leave bedroom doors open so no room becomes a pocket. Most families notice the smell drop sharply by the second morning.
If a newborn or an asthmatic child sleeps in a newly carpeted room, have them sleep elsewhere for the first two or three nights. Not because it is dangerous, because it is easy and removes the worry.
Any remaining smell is faint and mostly from the pad. If a strong odor persists past two weeks, something else is going on; see the warning below.

blocks.text: Choices that cut the smell before it starts

items.html: Insist on Green Label Plus carpet and Green Label pad. Both, not just the carpet. The pad is the piece most people forget to ask about.
Upgrade the pad to felt or a low-odor foam. A dense felt or fiber pad costs a little more than standard rebond, emits less, and often feels better underfoot in bedrooms. We bring pad samples too.
Stay with stretch-in installation. It uses no adhesive. Glue-down is for commercial spaces and a few specialty products; there is almost never a reason for it in a Sammamish home.

Consider wool for the nursery. Wool has a natural, faint lanolin smell rather than a chemical one, and takes no topical stain treatment. It costs more and is a poor choice in a damp basement, but for an upstairs bedroom it is the lowest-odor option there is.

Ask about solution-dyed fiber with no topical treatment. Solution-dyed nylon and triexta have color built into the fiber and need fewer surface chemicals. Some lines skip topical stain treatment entirely.

blocks.title: A smell that will not quit is not the carpet:
blocks.text: New carpet odor fades on a curve. If a musty or sharp smell is still strong after two weeks, or gets worse in wet weather, the usual causes are a damp slab or subfloor under the pad, an old pet-urine spot in the subfloor that the new carpet is now holding in, or a leak. Call us; we will pull a corner and look rather than guess.

faq.q: How long does new carpet smell last?
faq.a: Two to three days in a house with windows open or an HRV running, up to a week or two in a closed house in winter. The smell peaks in the first 24 hours and drops on a curve. If it is still strong after two weeks, suspect moisture under the pad or an old subfloor odor rather than the carpet.

faq.q: Is new carpet smell toxic to babies?
faq.a: The measured levels of 4-PC and other VOCs from certified carpet are far below health thresholds, and no study has tied new carpet odor to harm in infants. That said, a baby sleeps close to the floor, so it costs nothing to choose Green Label Plus carpet and pad and let the room air out for two or three nights first.

faq.q: What does Green Label Plus actually test?
faq.a: An independent lab places the carpet in a sealed chamber and measures total VOCs, 4-PC, formaldehyde and a list of individual compounds over 14 days. The carpet passes only if every one stays under the program's limits. The mark is on the sample back or spec sheet, and a separate Green Label exists for pad.

No. Emissions from carpet drop by well over 90 percent in the first two weeks and settle at background levels afterward. Old carpet does not emit VOCs in any meaningful amount; its air-quality issues, if any, come from dust, dander and moisture trapped in the pile, which is a cleaning question, not a chemical one.

faq.q: Is wool carpet lower VOC than nylon?
faq.a: Generally yes. Wool fiber needs no topical stain treatment and its faint natural smell is lanolin, not latex. But the backing on a wool broadloom can still use latex, so check for Green Label Plus regardless of fiber. Wool costs considerably more and does poorly in damp basements, so it is best for upstairs bedrooms.
